lessons.title: Fractions to Decimals and Place Value (Exercise 1)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A decimal is a fraction whose denominator is 10, 100 or 1000. Count the zeros in the denominator and place the decimal point that many digits from the right. Place values to the right of the decimal point are tenths (0.1), hundredths (0.01) and thousandths (0.001); to the left they are ones (1), tens (10) and hundreds (100). The place value of a digit = the digit x its place value.

Worked example: Write fractions as decimals (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 16/100: the denominator 100 has 2 zeros, so place the point 2 digits from the right: 16/100 = 0.16
Step 2: (b) 1/10: the denominator 10 has 1 zero, so place the point 1 digit from the right: 1/10 = 0.1
Step 3: (c) 324/1000: the denominator 1000 has 3 zeros, so place the point 3 digits from the right: 324/1000 = 0.324
Step 4: (d) 2/100: place the point 2 digits from the right and fill the empty tenths place with 0: 2/100 = 0.02
Step 5: (e) 70/1000: place the point 3 digits from the right: 70/1000 = 0.070
Answer: (a) 0.16, (b) 0.1, (c) 0.324, (d) 0.02, (e) 0.070

Worked example: Place value of the coloured digits (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: (a) In 1.56, 5 is at the tenths place: 5 x 0.1 = 0.5
Step 2: (b) In 45.987, 8 is at the hundredths place: 8 x 0.01 = 0.08
Step 3: (c) In 321.17, 3 is at the hundreds place: 3 x 100 = 300
Step 4: (d) In 6.897, 9 is at the hundredths place: 9 x 0.01 = 0.09
Step 5: (e) In 6.340, 0 is at the thousandths place: 0 x 0.001 = 0.000
Step 6: (f) In 12.123, 2 is at the ones place: 2 x 1 = 2
Step 7: (g) In 78.808, 8 is at the thousandths place: 8 x 0.001 = 0.008
Step 8: (h) In 4.009, 0 is at the tenths place: 0 x 0.1 = 0.0
Answer: (a) 0.5, (b) 0.08, (c) 300, (d) 0.09, (e) 0.000, (f) 2, (g) 0.008, (h) 0.0

Worked example: Colour the shapes for the given decimals (Exercise 1, Q3)

Step 1: Each shape is divided into 10 equal parts, so each part is 0.1
Step 2: (a) 0.2 = 2 parts out of 10: colour 2 parts
Step 3: (b) 0.7 = 7 parts out of 10: colour 7 parts
Step 4: (c) 0.9 = 9 parts out of 10: colour 9 parts
Answer: (a) colour 2 parts for 0.2, (b) colour 7 parts for 0.7, (c) colour 9 parts for 0.9

Worked example: Fill in the blanks with place values (Exercise 1, Q4)

Step 1: (a) 7.45: 7 is at ones place, 7 x 1 = 7; 4 is at tenths place, 4 x 0.1 = 0.4; 5 is at hundredths place, 5 x 0.01 = 0.05
Step 2: (b) 26.9: 2 is at tens place, 2 x 10 = 20; 6 is at ones place, 6 x 1 = 6; 9 is at tenths place, 9 x 0.1 = 0.9
Step 3: (c) 87.391: 8 is at tens place, 8 x 10 = 80; 7 is at ones place, 7 x 1 = 7; 3 is at tenths place, 3 x 0.1 = 0.3; 9 is at hundredths place, 9 x 0.01 = 0.09; 1 is at thousandths place, 1 x 0.001 = 0.001
Step 4: (d) 99.999: 9 is at tens place, 9 x 10 = 90; 9 is at ones place, 9 x 1 = 9; 9 is at tenths place, 9 x 0.1 = 0.9; 9 is at hundredths place, 9 x 0.01 = 0.09; 9 is at thousandths place, 9 x 0.001 = 0.009
Answer: (a) 7, 0.4, 0.05; (b) 20, 6, 0.9; (c) 80, 7, 0.3, 0.09, 0.001; (d) 90, 9, 0.9, 0.09, 0.009

Worked example: Place value of each digit in 200.149 (Try It!, book p75) (Try It!, book page 75)

Step 1: 2 is at hundreds place: 2 x 100 = 200
Step 2: 0 is at tens place: 0 x 10 = 0
Step 3: 0 is at ones place: 0 x 1 = 0
Step 4: 1 is at tenths place: 1 x 0.1 = 0.1
Step 5: 4 is at hundredths place: 4 x 0.01 = 0.04
Step 6: 9 is at thousandths place: 9 x 0.001 = 0.009
Step 7: Add the place values for the expanded form: 200 + 0 + 0 + 0.1 + 0.04 + 0.009
Answer: Expanded form: 200.149 = 200 + 0 + 0 + 0.1 + 0.04 + 0.009

lessons.title: Changing Fractions to Decimals and Decimals to Fractions (Exercise 2)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To change a fraction into a decimal, first make its denominator 10, 100 or 1000, then place the decimal point. To change a decimal into a fraction, write the digits after the point over 10, 100 or 1000 according to the number of decimal places, then divide the numerator and denominator by their common factor to get the lowest form.

Worked example: Represent the fractions as decimals (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 24/100 already has denominator 100: 24/100 = 0.24
Step 2: (b) 5/1000 already has denominator 1000: 5/1000 = 0.005
Step 3: (c) 6/10 already has denominator 10: 6/10 = 0.6
Step 4: (d) 12/500: multiply numerator and denominator by 2: 24/1000 = 0.024
Step 5: (e) 3/250: multiply numerator and denominator by 4: 12/1000 = 0.012
Step 6: (f) 47/25: multiply numerator and denominator by 4: 188/100 = 1.88
Step 7: (g) 60/200: divide numerator and denominator by 2: 30/100 = 0.3
Step 8: (h) 606/1000 already has denominator 1000: 606/1000 = 0.606
Step 9: (i) 80/1000 already has denominator 1000: 80/1000 = 0.08
Step 10: (j) 1/50: multiply numerator and denominator by 2: 2/100 = 0.02
Answer: (a) 0.24, (b) 0.005, (c) 0.6, (d) 0.024, (e) 0.012, (f) 1.88, (g) 0.3, (h) 0.606, (i) 0.08, (j) 0.02

Worked example: Convert decimals into fractions in lowest form (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: (a) 1.3 has 1 decimal place: 1.3 = 13/10 (already in lowest form)
Step 2: (b) 2.04 has 2 decimal places: 2.04 = 204/100; divide by 4: 51/25
Step 3: (c) 6.98 = 698/100; divide by 2: 349/50
Step 4: (d) 5.5 = 55/10; divide by 5: 11/2
Step 5: (e) 0.68 = 68/100; divide by 4: 17/25
Step 6: (f) 21.72 = 2172/100; divide by 4: 543/25
Step 7: (g) 7.87 = 787/100 (already in lowest form)
Step 8: (h) 0.98 = 98/100; divide by 2: 49/50
Step 9: (i) 11.11 = 1111/100 (already in lowest form)
Step 10: (j) 6.10 = 610/100; divide by 10: 61/10
Answer: (a) 13/10, (b) 51/25, (c) 349/50, (d) 11/2, (e) 17/25, (f) 543/25, (g) 787/100, (h) 49/50, (i) 1111/100, (j) 61/10

Worked example: Show 7.74 in the place value chart and as a fraction (Try It!, book p79) (Try It!, book page 79)

Step 1: 7 before the point is at ones place: 7 x 1 = 7
Step 2: The first 7 after the point is at tenths place: 7 x 0.1 = 0.7
Step 3: 4 is at hundredths place: 4 x 0.01 = 0.04
Step 4: Write 7.74 as a fraction: 7.74 = 774/100
Step 5: Divide numerator and denominator by 2 for the lowest form: 774/100 = 387/50
Answer: Ones 7, tenths 7, hundredths 4; 7.74 = 774/100 = 387/50

mcqs.q: 12/500 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: First make the denominator 1000: multiply the numerator and denominator by 2: 12 x 2 = 24 and 500 x 2 = 1000. So 12/500 = 24/1000 = 0.024.

mcqs.q: 47/25 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 4: 47 x 4 = 188 and 25 x 4 = 100. So 47/25 = 188/100 = 1.88.

mcqs.q: 0.68 as a fraction in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 0.68 has 2 decimal places, so 0.68 = 68/100. Divide the numerator and denominator by 4: 68 / 4 = 17 and 100 / 4 = 25, giving 17/25.

mcqs.q: 5.5 as a fraction in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 5.5 = 55/10. Divide the numerator and denominator by 5: 55 / 5 = 11 and 10 / 5 = 2, giving 11/2.

mcqs.q: 60/200 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: Divide the numerator and denominator by 2: 60 / 2 = 30 and 200 / 2 = 100. So 60/200 = 30/100 = 0.3.

mcqs.q: 2.04 as a fraction in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 2.04 = 204/100. Divide the numerator and denominator by 4: 204 / 4 = 51 and 100 / 4 = 25, giving 51/25.

mcqs.q: 5/1000 as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: The denominator 1000 has 3 zeros, so place the point 3 digits from the right and fill the empty places with zeros: 5/1000 = 0.005.

mcqs.q: 6.10 as a fraction in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 6.10 = 610/100. Divide the numerator and denominator by 10: 610 / 10 = 61 and 100 / 10 = 10, giving 61/10.

mcqs.q: 7.74 as a fraction in lowest form is:
mcqs.why: 7.74 = 774/100. Divide the numerator and denominator by 2: 774 / 2 = 387 and 100 / 2 = 50, giving 387/50.

mcqs.q: To change a decimal into a fraction, we write the digits after the point over:
options: 10, 100 or 1000 according to the number of decimal places
mcqs.why: The denominator depends on the decimal places: 1 place means over 10, 2 places over 100 and 3 places over 1000. Then divide by the common factor for the lowest form.

lessons.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals (Exercise 3)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Always line up the decimal points. Add or subtract ones in ones, tenths in tenths and hundredths in hundredths, starting from the smallest place and carrying or borrowing when needed. Keep the decimal point in the answer in the same column.

Worked example: Add the decimals (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 9.11 + 8.03: add hundredths 1 + 3 = 4, tenths 1 + 0 = 1, ones 9 + 8 = 17: 17.14
Step 2: (b) 43.1 + 12.7: add tenths 1 + 7 = 8, ones 3 + 2 = 5, tens 4 + 1 = 5: 55.8
Step 3: (c) 52.9 + 2.2: add tenths 9 + 2 = 11 tenths, write 1 and carry 1; ones 2 + 2 + 1 = 5, tens 5: 55.1
Step 4: (d) 5.69 + 2.98: add hundredths 9 + 8 = 17, write 7 carry 1; tenths 6 + 9 + 1 = 16, write 6 carry 1; ones 5 + 2 + 1 = 8: 8.67
Step 5: (e) 6.02 + 1.89: add hundredths 2 + 9 = 11, write 1 carry 1; tenths 0 + 8 + 1 = 9; ones 6 + 1 = 7: 7.91
Step 6: (f) 49.3 + 21.6: add tenths 3 + 6 = 9, ones 9 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1; tens 4 + 2 + 1 = 7: 70.9
Answer: (a) 17.14, (b) 55.8, (c) 55.1, (d) 8.67, (e) 7.91, (f) 70.9

Worked example: Subtract the decimals (Exercise 3, Q2)

Step 1: (a) 4.91 - 3.92: hundredths 1 - 2 cannot be done, borrow 1 tenth: 11 - 2 = 9; tenths 8 - 9 cannot be done, borrow 1 one: 18 - 9 = 9; ones 3 - 3 = 0: 0.99
Step 2: (b) 7.34 - 2.86: hundredths 4 - 6, borrow: 14 - 6 = 8; tenths 2 - 8, borrow: 12 - 8 = 4; ones 6 - 2 = 4: 4.48
Step 3: (c) 5.06 - 2.76: hundredths 6 - 6 = 0; tenths 0 - 7, borrow 1 one: 10 - 7 = 3; ones 4 - 2 = 2: 2.30
Step 4: (d) 7.88 - 6.19: hundredths 8 - 9, borrow: 18 - 9 = 9; tenths 7 - 1 = 6; ones 7 - 6 = 1: 1.69
Step 5: (e) 9.80 - 1.09: hundredths 0 - 9, borrow 1 tenth: 10 - 9 = 1; tenths 7 - 0 = 7; ones 9 - 1 = 8: 8.71
Step 6: (f) 78.9 - 7.84: write 78.9 as 78.90; hundredths 0 - 4, borrow: 10 - 4 = 6; tenths 8 - 8 = 0; ones 8 - 7 = 1, tens 7: 71.06
Answer: (a) 0.99, (b) 4.48, (c) 2.30, (d) 1.69, (e) 8.71, (f) 71.06

Worked example: Zubair's spending on a chocolate and a candy (Exercise 3, Q3)

Step 1: Altogether means add: 45.7 + 10.2
Step 2: Add the tenths: 7 + 2 = 9 tenths
Step 3: Add the ones and tens: 45 + 10 = 55
Step 4: Put the parts together: 55 and 9 tenths = 55.9
Answer: Rs 55.9

Worked example: Mass of apples and guavas: difference and total (Exercise 3, Q4)

Step 1: Apples = 38.9 kg, guavas = 42.6 kg; guavas are heavier
Step 2: (a) Difference = 42.6 - 38.9: tenths 6 - 9, borrow: 16 - 9 = 7; ones 1 - 8, borrow: 11 - 8 = 3: 3.7 kg
Step 3: (b) Total = 38.9 + 42.6: tenths 9 + 6 = 15, write 5 carry 1; ones 8 + 2 + 1 = 11, write 1 carry 1; tens 3 + 4 + 1 = 8: 81.5 kg
Answer: (a) 3.7 kg, (b) 81.5 kg

Worked example: Find the missing decimal in a sum (Try It!, book p82) (Try It!, book page 82)

Step 1: The sum of two decimals is 12.8 and the second decimal is 7.9
Step 2: First decimal = sum - second decimal = 12.8 - 7.9
Step 3: Tenths: 8 - 9, borrow 1 one: 18 - 9 = 9; ones: 11 - 7 = 4: first decimal = 4.9
Step 4: To get 25.8 from 12.8, subtract: 25.8 - 12.8 = 13.0
Answer: First decimal fraction = 4.9; add 13.0 to 12.8 to get 25.8

mcqs.q: 9.11 + 8.03 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Line up the decimal points. Hundredths: 1 + 3 = 4. Tenths: 1 + 0 = 1. Ones: 9 + 8 = 17. The sum is 17.14.

mcqs.q: 5.69 + 2.98 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Hundredths: 9 + 8 = 17, write 7 and carry 1. Tenths: 6 + 9 + 1 = 16, write 6 and carry 1. Ones: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8. The sum is 8.67.

mcqs.q: 4.91 - 3.92 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Hundredths: 1 - 2 cannot be done, so borrow 1 tenth: 11 - 2 = 9. Tenths: 8 - 9 cannot be done, so borrow 1 one: 18 - 9 = 9. Ones: 3 - 3 = 0. The difference is 0.99.

mcqs.q: 7.34 - 2.86 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Hundredths: borrow 1 tenth: 14 - 6 = 8. Tenths: borrow 1 one: 12 - 8 = 4. Ones: 6 - 2 = 4. The difference is 4.48.

mcqs.q: Zubair spends Rs 45.7 on a chocolate and Rs 10.2 on a candy. How much does he spend altogether?
mcqs.why: Altogether means add: 45.7 + 10.2. Add the tenths: 7 + 2 = 9 tenths. Add the ones and tens: 45 + 10 = 55. He spends Rs 55.9 in total.

mcqs.q: Apples weigh 38.9 kg and guavas weigh 42.6 kg. The difference between their masses is:
mcqs.why: Difference: 42.6 - 38.9. Tenths: borrow 1 one: 16 - 9 = 7. Ones: borrow 1 ten: 11 - 8 = 3. The difference is 3.7 kg, and the guavas are heavier.

mcqs.q: The total mass of the apples (38.9 kg) and guavas (42.6 kg) is:
mcqs.why: Total: 38.9 + 42.6. Tenths: 9 + 6 = 15, write 5 and carry 1. Ones: 8 + 2 + 1 = 11, write 1 and carry 1. Tens: 3 + 4 + 1 = 8. The total mass is 81.5 kg.

mcqs.q: 78.9 - 7.84 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Write 78.9 as 78.90 so the decimal points line up. Hundredths: borrow: 10 - 4 = 6. Tenths: 8 - 8 = 0. Ones: 8 - 7 = 1 and tens: 7. The difference is 71.06.

mcqs.q: The sum of two decimals is 12.8 and the second decimal is 7.9. The first decimal is:
mcqs.why: First decimal = sum - second decimal: 12.8 - 7.9. Tenths: borrow 1 one: 18 - 9 = 9. Ones: 11 - 7 = 4. The first decimal is 4.9.

mcqs.q: 49.3 + 21.6 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Tenths: 3 + 6 = 9. Ones: 9 + 1 = 10, write 0 and carry 1. Tens: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. The sum is 70.9.

lessons.title: Multiplying and Dividing Decimals (Exercise 4)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

When we multiply a decimal by 10, move the decimal point 1 place to the right; by 100, move it 2 places to the right; by 1000, move it 3 places to the right. To multiply or divide a decimal by a whole number, work as with whole numbers and keep the decimal point in line in the answer.

Worked example: Multiply decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 (Exercise 4, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 5.9 x 10: move the point 1 place right: 59
Step 2: (b) 4.8 x 100: move the point 2 places right and add a 0: 480
Step 3: (c) 0.3 x 1000: move the point 3 places right and add zeros: 300
Step 4: (d) 8.2 x 10: move the point 1 place right: 82
Step 5: (e) 4.3 x 1000: move the point 3 places right and add zeros: 4300
Step 6: (f) 9.1 x 100: move the point 2 places right and add a 0: 910
Answer: (a) 59, (b) 480, (c) 300, (d) 82, (e) 4300, (f) 910

Worked example: Multiply decimals by whole numbers (Exercise 4, Q2)

Step 1: (a) 5.6 x 8: 56 x 8 = 448, place the point 1 digit from the right: 44.8
Step 2: (b) 7.1 x 2: 71 x 2 = 142, place the point: 14.2
Step 3: (c) 4.9 x 4: 49 x 4 = 196, place the point: 19.6
Step 4: (d) 3.4 x 3: 34 x 3 = 102, place the point: 10.2
Step 5: (e) 1.3 x 7: 13 x 7 = 91, place the point: 9.1
Step 6: (f) 9.8 x 9: 98 x 9 = 882, place the point: 88.2
Answer: (a) 44.8, (b) 14.2, (c) 19.6, (d) 10.2, (e) 9.1, (f) 88.2

Worked example: Divide decimals by whole numbers (Exercise 4, Q3)

Step 1: (a) 1.4 / 2: 14 tenths / 2 = 7 tenths: 0.7
Step 2: (b) 1.8 / 9: 18 tenths / 9 = 2 tenths: 0.2
Step 3: (c) 6.4 / 4: 6 / 4 = 1 remainder 2; 24 tenths / 4 = 6 tenths: 1.6
Step 4: (d) 8.4 / 6: 8 / 6 = 1 remainder 2; 24 tenths / 6 = 4 tenths: 1.4
Step 5: (e) 2.7 / 3: 27 tenths / 3 = 9 tenths: 0.9
Step 6: (f) 2.6 / 2: 2 / 2 = 1; 6 tenths / 2 = 3 tenths: 1.3
Answer: (a) 0.7, (b) 0.2, (c) 1.6, (d) 1.4, (e) 0.9, (f) 1.3

Worked example: Oil used for 10 cakes (Exercise 4, Q4)

Step 1: Oil for 1 cake = 9.8 ml
Step 2: Oil for 10 cakes = 9.8 x 10
Step 3: Move the decimal point 1 place to the right: 9.8 x 10 = 98
Answer: 98 ml

Worked example: Cloth used for 8 shirts (Exercise 4, Q5)

Step 1: Cloth for 1 shirt = 2.5 m
Step 2: Cloth for 8 shirts = 2.5 x 8
Step 3: 25 x 8 = 200, place the point 1 digit from the right: 20.0 = 20
Answer: 20 m

Worked example: Cutting a 7.2 m rope into equal pieces (Exercise 4, Q6)

Step 1: (a) Length of each of 4 pieces = 7.2 / 4: 7 / 4 = 1 remainder 3; 32 tenths / 4 = 8 tenths: 1.8 m
Step 2: (b) Length of each of 2 pieces = 7.2 / 2: 7 / 2 = 3 remainder 1; 12 tenths / 2 = 6 tenths: 3.6 m
Answer: (a) 1.8 m per piece, (b) 3.6 m per piece

Worked example: Time Ahmed takes for 1 question (Exercise 4, Q7)

Step 1: 5 questions take 8.5 minutes
Step 2: Time for 1 question = 8.5 / 5
Step 3: 8 / 5 = 1 remainder 3; 35 tenths / 5 = 7 tenths: 1.7
Answer: 1.7 minutes

Worked example: Divide 2.8 by 4 and find decimals that give 1.2, 0.2 and 0.4 (Try It!, book p85) (Try It!, book page 85)

Step 1: 2.8 / 4: 28 tenths / 4 = 7 tenths: 0.7
Step 2: To find a decimal which divided by 4 gives 1.2, multiply back: 1.2 x 4 = 4.8
Step 3: For 0.2: 0.2 x 4 = 0.8
Step 4: For 0.4: 0.4 x 4 = 1.6
Answer: 2.8 / 4 = 0.7; the decimals are 4.8, 0.8 and 1.6

mcqs.q: 5.9 x 10 is equal to:
mcqs.why: When we multiply a decimal by 10, the decimal point moves 1 place to the right: 5.9 x 10 = 59.

mcqs.q: 0.3 x 1000 is equal to:
mcqs.why: When we multiply by 1000, the point moves 3 places to the right and zeros are added: 0.3 x 1000 = 300.

mcqs.q: 4.8 x 100 is equal to:
mcqs.why: When we multiply by 100, the point moves 2 places to the right and a 0 is added: 4.8 x 100 = 480.

mcqs.q: 5.6 x 8 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Work as with whole numbers: 56 x 8 = 448. The decimal has 1 decimal place, so place the point 1 digit from the right: 5.6 x 8 = 44.8.

mcqs.q: 1.4 / 2 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Divide using tenths: 14 tenths / 2 = 7 tenths, so 1.4 / 2 = 0.7.

mcqs.q: 6.4 / 4 is equal to:
mcqs.why: 6 / 4 gives quotient 1 and remainder 2; then 24 tenths / 4 = 6 tenths. So 6.4 / 4 = 1.6.

mcqs.q: Oil used for 1 cake is 9.8 ml. The oil used for 10 cakes is:
mcqs.why: Multiply by 10: move the decimal point 1 place to the right: 9.8 x 10 = 98. The oil used for 10 cakes is 98 ml.

mcqs.q: Cloth used for 1 shirt is 2.5 m. The cloth used for 8 shirts is:
mcqs.why: Multiply: 2.5 x 8. 25 x 8 = 200, and placing the point 1 digit from the right gives 20.0, which is 20 m.

mcqs.q: A 7.2 m rope is cut into 4 equal pieces. The length of each piece is:
mcqs.why: Divide: 7.2 / 4. 7 / 4 gives quotient 1 and remainder 3; then 32 tenths / 4 = 8 tenths. Each piece is 1.8 m long.

mcqs.q: Ahmed solves 5 questions in 8.5 minutes. The time he takes for 1 question is:
mcqs.why: Divide: 8.5 / 5. 8 / 5 gives quotient 1 and remainder 3; then 35 tenths / 5 = 7 tenths. He takes 1.7 minutes for 1 question.

lessons.title: Rounding Off Numbers and Decimals (Exercise 5)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Round off means to find a number that is nearest to the original number but not exact. To round to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000, look at the next digit: if it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, round down. To round a decimal to the nearest whole number, look at the digit after the decimal point in the same way.

Worked example: Round whole numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (Exercise 5, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 9871: ones digit 1, round down to 9870; tens digit 7, round up to 9900; hundreds digit 8, round up to 10000
Step 2: (b) 5467: 5470 (7 rounds up), 5500 (6 rounds up), 5000 (4 rounds down)
Step 3: (c) 1212: 1210 (2 rounds down), 1200 (1 rounds down), 1000 (2 rounds down)
Step 4: (d) 6343: 6340 (3 rounds down), 6300 (4 rounds down), 6000 (3 rounds down)
Step 5: (e) 5555: 5560 (5 rounds up), 5600 (5 rounds up), 6000 (5 rounds up)
Step 6: (f) 3498: 3500 (8 rounds up), 3500 (9 rounds up), 3000 (4 rounds down)
Step 7: (g) 1289: 1290 (9 rounds up), 1300 (8 rounds up), 1000 (2 rounds down)
Step 8: (h) 4545: 4550 (5 rounds up), 4500 (4 rounds down), 5000 (5 rounds up)
Step 9: (i) 1111: 1110 (1 rounds down), 1100 (1 rounds down), 1000 (1 rounds down)
Answer: (a) 9870, 9900, 10000; (b) 5470, 5500, 5000; (c) 1210, 1200, 1000; (d) 6340, 6300, 6000; (e) 5560, 5600, 6000; (f) 3500, 3500, 3000; (g) 1290, 1300, 1000; (h) 4550, 4500, 5000; (i) 1110, 1100, 1000

Worked example: Round decimals to the nearest whole number (Exercise 5, Q2)

Step 1: Look at the tenths digit of each decimal: 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 rounds down
Step 2: (a) 5.61: tenths digit 6, round up: 6
Step 3: (b) 54.2: tenths digit 2, round down: 54
Step 4: (c) 987.4: tenths digit 4, round down: 987
Step 5: (d) 12.7: tenths digit 7, round up: 13
Step 6: (e) 8.98: tenths digit 9, round up: 9
Step 7: (f) 6.5: tenths digit 5, round up: 7
Step 8: (g) 76.4: tenths digit 4, round down: 76
Step 9: (h) 8.19: tenths digit 1, round down: 8
Step 10: (i) 87.87: tenths digit 8, round up: 88
Answer: (a) 6, (b) 54, (c) 987, (d) 13, (e) 9, (f) 7, (g) 76, (h) 8, (i) 88

Worked example: Write 3 decimals which round off to 68 (Try It!, book p89) (Try It!, book page 89)

Step 1: A decimal rounds to 68 if it is from 67.5 up to 68.4
Step 2: 67.5: tenths digit 5, rounds up to 68
Step 3: 67.9: tenths digit 9, rounds up to 68
Step 4: 68.2: tenths digit 2, rounds down to 68
Answer: 67.5, 67.9 and 68.2 (model answers)

mcqs.q: To round off a number, if the next digit is 5 or more, we:
mcqs.why: The rounding rule: look at the next digit. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, round down.

mcqs.q: 9871 rounded to the nearest 1000 is:
mcqs.why: Look at the hundreds digit of 9871: 8 is 5 or more, so round up. 9871 rounds to 10000 to the nearest 1000.

mcqs.q: 5467 rounded to the nearest 10 is:
mcqs.why: Look at the ones digit of 5467: 7 is 5 or more, so round up the tens digit. 5467 rounds to 5470 to the nearest 10.

mcqs.q: 1212 rounded to the nearest 100 is:
mcqs.why: Look at the tens digit of 1212: 1 is less than 5, so round down. 1212 rounds to 1200 to the nearest 100.

mcqs.q: 5555 rounded to the nearest 1000 is:
mcqs.why: Look at the hundreds digit of 5555: 5 means round up. 5555 rounds to 6000 to the nearest 1000.

mcqs.q: 5.61 rounded to the nearest whole number is:
mcqs.why: Look at the tenths digit of 5.61: 6 is 5 or more, so round up. 5.61 rounds to 6.

mcqs.q: 54.2 rounded to the nearest whole number is:
mcqs.why: Look at the tenths digit of 54.2: 2 is less than 5, so round down. 54.2 rounds to 54.

mcqs.q: 6.5 rounded to the nearest whole number is:
mcqs.why: The tenths digit of 6.5 is 5, and 5 or more means round up. 6.5 rounds to 7.

mcqs.q: Which decimal rounds off to 68?
mcqs.why: A decimal rounds to 68 if it is from 67.5 up to 68.4. 67.5 has tenths digit 5, so it rounds up to 68. 67.4 rounds down to 67, and 68.5 rounds up to 69.

mcqs.q: 87.87 rounded to the nearest whole number is:
mcqs.why: Look at the tenths digit of 87.87: 8 is 5 or more, so round up. 87.87 rounds to 88.

lessons.title: Length: Choosing Units and Converting (Exercise 1)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Length is measured in millimetres (mm), centimetres (cm), metres (m) and kilometres (km). 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm. A short object is measured in cm, a long object in m, and a distance between places in km. To convert a bigger unit into a smaller unit, multiply.

Worked example: Tick the correct units of length for the pictured objects (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: The four objects in this question are pictures in the book, so read each object from the book's picture and choose its unit from the choices given (m/cm, mm/cm, m/cm, m/km)
Step 2: A short object is measured in cm, a long object in m, and a distance between places in km
Step 3: From the book's answer list: object (a) takes cm
Step 4: Object (b) takes cm
Step 5: Object (c) takes m
Step 6: Object (d) takes km
Answer: (a) cm, (b) cm, (c) m, (d) km (picture items — the objects are pictures in the book)

Worked example: Convert the units of length (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: (a) 12 km into m: 12 x 1000 = 12000 m
Step 2: (b) 56 km 930 m into m: 56 x 1000 = 56000 m; 56000 + 930 = 56930 m
Step 3: (c) 88 m into cm: 88 x 100 = 8800 cm
Step 4: (d) 60 m 78 cm into cm: 60 x 100 = 6000 cm; 6000 + 78 = 6078 cm
Step 5: (e) 3.2 cm into mm: 3.2 x 10 = 32 mm
Step 6: (f) 55 cm 2 mm into mm: 55 x 10 = 550 mm; 550 + 2 = 552 mm
Answer: (a) 12000 m, (b) 56930 m, (c) 8800 cm, (d) 6078 cm, (e) 32 mm, (f) 552 mm

mcqs.q: 1 km is equal to:
mcqs.why: The length units are joined by: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm and 1 cm = 10 mm.

mcqs.q: 12 km in metres is:
mcqs.why: To convert a bigger unit into a smaller unit, multiply: 12 x 1000 = 12000. So 12 km = 12000 m.

mcqs.q: 56 km 930 m in metres is:
mcqs.why: Convert the km first: 56 x 1000 = 56000 m. Then add the metres: 56000 + 930 = 56930 m.

mcqs.q: 88 m in centimetres is:
mcqs.why: 1 m = 100 cm, so multiply by 100: 88 x 100 = 8800. So 88 m = 8800 cm.

mcqs.q: 60 m 78 cm in centimetres is:
mcqs.why: Convert the m first: 60 x 100 = 6000 cm. Then add the centimetres: 6000 + 78 = 6078 cm.

mcqs.q: 3.2 cm in millimetres is:
mcqs.why: 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply by 10: 3.2 x 10 = 32. So 3.2 cm = 32 mm.

mcqs.q: 55 cm 2 mm in millimetres is:
mcqs.why: Convert the cm first: 55 x 10 = 550 mm. Then add the millimetres: 550 + 2 = 552 mm.

mcqs.q: The distance between two places is best measured in:
mcqs.why: A short object is measured in cm, a long object in m, and a distance between places in km.

mcqs.q: To convert a bigger unit of length into a smaller unit, we:
mcqs.why: Converting from a bigger unit to a smaller unit always means multiplying: by 1000 for km to m, by 100 for m to cm and by 10 for cm to mm.

mcqs.q: 1 m is equal to:
mcqs.why: 1 m = 100 cm. Also 1 cm = 10 mm, so 1 m has 1000 mm, not 100 mm.

lessons.title: Length: Adding and Subtracting (Exercise 2)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Add or subtract lengths column by column in the same unit: km with km, m with m, cm with cm and mm with mm. 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm.

Worked example: Add the lengths (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 22 km + 33 km = 55 km
Step 2: (b) 88 km + 6 km 17 m: add km: 88 + 6 = 94 km; the 17 m stays: 94 km 17 m
Step 3: (c) 82 m + 22 m = 104 m
Step 4: (d) 71 cm 2 mm + 11 cm 6 mm: add mm: 2 + 6 = 8 mm; add cm: 71 + 11 = 82 cm: 82 cm 8 mm
Step 5: (e) 21 m 16 cm + 20 m 14 cm: add cm: 16 + 14 = 30 cm; add m: 21 + 20 = 41 m: 41 m 30 cm
Step 6: (f) 74 km 122 m + 13 m: add m: 122 + 13 = 135 m; km stays 74: 74 km 135 m
Answer: (a) 55 km, (b) 94 km 17 m, (c) 104 m, (d) 82 cm 8 mm, (e) 41 m 30 cm, (f) 74 km 135 m

Worked example: Subtract the lengths (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: (a) 99 km - 74 km = 25 km
Step 2: (b) 52 km 48 m - 6 km 22 m: subtract m: 48 - 22 = 26 m; subtract km: 52 - 6 = 46 km: 46 km 26 m
Step 3: (c) 47 m - 10 m = 37 m
Step 4: (d) 35 cm 5 mm - 25 cm 1 mm: subtract mm: 5 - 1 = 4 mm; subtract cm: 35 - 25 = 10 cm: 10 cm 4 mm
Step 5: (e) 21 m 16 cm - 20 m 14 cm: subtract cm: 16 - 14 = 2 cm; subtract m: 21 - 20 = 1 m: 1 m 2 cm
Step 6: (f) 74 km 122 m - 13 m: subtract m: 122 - 13 = 109 m; km stays 74: 74 km 109 m
Answer: (a) 25 km, (b) 46 km 26 m, (c) 37 m, (d) 10 cm 4 mm, (e) 1 m 2 cm, (f) 74 km 109 m

Worked example: Total length of Tahir's two pieces of rope (Exercise 2, Q3)

Step 1: Total length = 38 m 87 cm + 61 m 12 cm
Step 2: Add the cm: 87 + 12 = 99 cm
Step 3: Add the m: 38 + 61 = 99 m
Step 4: Write the two parts together
Answer: 99 m 99 cm

Worked example: Convert Ahmed's 140 cm ribbon into millimetres (Exercise 2, Q4)

Step 1: 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply by 10
Step 2: 140 cm = 140 x 10 = 1400 mm
Answer: 1400 mm

Worked example: Kamal's two distances: difference in km and m, then in metres (Exercise 2, Q5)

Step 1: (a) Difference = 2 km 712 m - 1 km 216 m
Step 2: Subtract the m: 712 - 216 = 496 m
Step 3: Subtract the km: 2 - 1 = 1 km: difference = 1 km 496 m
Step 4: (b) Convert into metres: 1 km = 1000 m, so 1 km 496 m = 1000 + 496 = 1496 m
Answer: (a) 1 km 496 m, (b) 1496 m

Worked example: Ahmed's room and his sister's room: total in cm and difference (Exercise 2, Q6)

Step 1: (a) Total = 5 m 56 cm + 4 m 44 cm: add cm: 56 + 44 = 100 cm; add m: 5 + 4 = 9 m: 9 m 100 cm
Step 2: 100 cm = 1 m, so 9 m 100 cm = 10 m
Step 3: Convert into cm: 10 m = 10 x 100 = 1000 cm
Step 4: (b) Difference = 5 m 56 cm - 4 m 44 cm: subtract cm: 56 - 44 = 12 cm; subtract m: 5 - 4 = 1 m: 1 m 12 cm
Answer: (a) 1000 cm, (b) 1 m 12 cm

mcqs.q: 71 cm 2 mm + 11 cm 6 mm is equal to:
mcqs.why: Add lengths in the same unit: mm: 2 + 6 = 8 mm; cm: 71 + 11 = 82 cm. The sum is 82 cm 8 mm.

mcqs.q: 52 km 48 m - 6 km 22 m is equal to:
mcqs.why: Subtract in the same unit: m: 48 - 22 = 26 m; km: 52 - 6 = 46 km. The difference is 46 km 26 m.

mcqs.q: 21 m 16 cm + 20 m 14 cm is equal to:
mcqs.why: Add in the same unit: cm: 16 + 14 = 30 cm; m: 21 + 20 = 41 m. The sum is 41 m 30 cm.

mcqs.q: 35 cm 5 mm - 25 cm 1 mm is equal to:
mcqs.why: Subtract in the same unit: mm: 5 - 1 = 4 mm; cm: 35 - 25 = 10 cm. The difference is 10 cm 4 mm.

mcqs.q: Tahir has two pieces of rope: 38 m 87 cm and 61 m 12 cm. Their total length is:
mcqs.why: Add the cm: 87 + 12 = 99 cm. Add the m: 38 + 61 = 99 m. The total length of the two pieces is 99 m 99 cm.

mcqs.q: Ahmed has a ribbon 140 cm long. Its length in millimetres is:
mcqs.why: 1 cm = 10 mm, so multiply by 10: 140 x 10 = 1400. The ribbon is 1400 mm long.

mcqs.q: Kamal's two distances are 2 km 712 m and 1 km 216 m. Their difference is:
mcqs.why: Subtract the m: 712 - 216 = 496 m. Subtract the km: 2 - 1 = 1 km. The difference is 1 km 496 m.

mcqs.q: The difference 1 km 496 m written in metres is:
Ahmed's room is 5 m 56 cm long and his sister's room is 4 m 44 cm. Their total length in centimetres is:
mcqs.why: Add: cm: 56 + 44 = 100 cm; m: 5 + 4 = 9 m, giving 9 m 100 cm. Since 100 cm = 1 m, this is 10 m, and 10 x 100 = 1000 cm.

mcqs.q: The difference between the two rooms (5 m 56 cm and 4 m 44 cm) is:
mcqs.why: Subtract the cm: 56 - 44 = 12 cm. Subtract the m: 5 - 4 = 1 m. The difference is 1 m 12 cm.

lessons.title: Mass: Converting, Adding and Subtracting (Exercise 3)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Mass is measured in milligrams (mg), grams (g) and kilograms (kg). 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 g = 1000 mg. To convert a bigger unit into a smaller unit, multiply by 1000. Add or subtract mass column by column in the same unit.

Worked example: Convert the units of mass (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: (a) 65 kg into g: 65 x 1000 = 65000 g
Step 2: (b) 23 kg 139 g into g: 23 x 1000 = 23000 g; 23000 + 139 = 23139 g
Step 3: (c) 89 g into mg: 89 x 1000 = 89000 mg
Step 4: (d) 43 g 699 mg into mg: 43 x 1000 = 43000 mg; 43000 + 699 = 43699 mg
Step 5: (e) 1.9 g into mg: 1.9 x 1000 = 1900 mg
Step 6: (f) 0.8 kg into g: 0.8 x 1000 = 800 g
Answer: (a) 65000 g, (b) 23139 g, (c) 89000 mg, (d) 43699 mg, (e) 1900 mg, (f) 800 g

Worked example: Add the masses (Exercise 3, Q2)

Step 1: (a) 36 kg + 76 kg = 112 kg
Step 2: (b) 18 kg + 17 kg 17 g: add kg: 18 + 17 = 35 kg; the 17 g stays: 35 kg 17 g
Step 3: (c) 8.2 g + 2.2 g = 10.4 g

lessons.title: Reading Clocks: 12-Hour and 24-Hour Time (Exercise 1)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A clock has an hour hand, a minute hand and a second hand. In the 12-hour clock we write a.m. for times after midnight and before noon, and p.m. for times after noon and before midnight. In the 24-hour clock the hours run from 0 to 23, so afternoon times add 12 to the hour. Time is written as hours : minutes : seconds.

Worked example: Colour the correct time of daily activities (12-hour clock) (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: Read each activity and pick its usual time in 12-hour format, as given in the book
Step 2: (a) Getting up for school: morning time, so a.m.: 6:00 a.m.
Step 3: (b) Going to school: morning time, so a.m.: 7:45 a.m.
Step 4: (c) Lunch time in school: after noon, so p.m.: 12:30 p.m.
Step 5: (d) Playing time in the evening: after noon, so p.m.: 4:30 p.m.
Step 6: (e) Isha Salah: night time, so p.m.: 8:00 p.m.
Step 7: (f) Sleeping time at night: p.m.: 10:25 p.m.
Answer: (a) 6:00 a.m., (b) 7:45 a.m., (c) 12:30 p.m., (d) 4:30 p.m., (e) 8:00 p.m., (f) 10:25 p.m.

Worked example: Write the clock times in 24-hour format (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: Read the hour, minute and second hands on each clock face in the book and write the time as hours : minutes : seconds
Step 2: (a) Numan takes his breakfast: the book's clock face reads 7:30:15

Step 4: (c) Junaid goes to sleep: the book's clock face reads 8:59:58
Answer: (a) 7:30:15, (b) 5:30:35, (c) 8:59:58 (read from the book's clock pictures)

mcqs.why: In the 24-hour clock the hours run from 0 to 23, so afternoon times add 12 to the hour of the 12-hour clock.

mcqs.why: Time is written as hours : minutes : seconds, for example 7:30:15 means 7 hours, 30 minutes and 15 seconds.

mcqs.why: Reading hours : minutes : seconds in 7:30:15: the hours are 7, the minutes are 30 and the seconds are 15.

mcqs.why: A clock has an hour hand, a minute hand and a second hand. The second hand shows the seconds; time is read hour first, then minutes, then seconds.

lessons.title: Exercise 1: Parallel and Non-Parallel Lines
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Parallel lines are straight lines that keep going in the same direction and never meet, however far they are extended. The distance between them is always the same. Non-parallel lines are lines that meet, or would meet if they were extended. To decide, look at the direction of each pair: same direction and same distance apart means parallel; different direction means non-parallel.

lessons.title: Exercise 2: Angles — Types, Measuring and Constructing
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

An angle is measured in degrees. An acute angle is less than 90 degrees. A right angle is equal to 90 degrees. An obtuse angle is greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees. A protractor is used to measure and to construct angles: place the centre point of the protractor on the vertex (for measuring) or on the end point of a ray (for constructing), place its baseline on the ray, and read or mark the required degree on the correct scale.

Angle types in words: an acute angle is a narrow opening, smaller than a square corner; a right angle is exactly a square corner; an obtuse angle is a wide opening, larger than a square corner but smaller than a straight line.

Worked example: Types of angles (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: Figure (a) is less than 90 degrees.
Step 2: So (a) is an acute angle.
Step 3: Figure (b) is equal to 90 degrees.
Step 4: So (b) is a right angle.
Step 5: Figure (c) is greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees.
Step 6: So (c) is an obtuse angle.
Step 7: Figure (d) is less than 90 degrees.
Step 8: So (d) is an acute angle.
Answer: (a) Acute angle, (b) Right angle, (c) Obtuse angle, (d) Acute angle.

Worked example: Measure angles with a protractor (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: This is a protractor figure activity. The angles are printed figures in the book.
Step 2: Place the centre point of the protractor on the vertex of the angle.
Step 3: Place the baseline of the protractor on the initial ray of the angle.
Step 4: Read the measure of the angle on the correct scale of the protractor.
Step 5: Write down the measure you read for each printed angle.
Step 6: Honest note: no text values are printed in the book or in its answer list for this question, so no degree values are given here. The angles must be measured from the printed figures with a protractor.
Answer: Measure each printed angle with a protractor as in Steps 2 to 4; the measures are read from the printed figures (no text values are given in the book).

Worked example: Construct angles of 60 degrees, 30 degrees and 115 degrees (Exercise 2, Q3)

Step 1: Draw a ray.
Step 2: Place the centre point of the protractor on the end point of the ray.
Step 3: Place the baseline of the protractor on the ray.
Step 4: For part (a), mark 60 degrees on the scale, remove the protractor, and join the mark to the end point of the ray.
Step 5: For part (b), repeat the same steps and mark 30 degrees on the scale, then join the mark to the end point.
Step 6: For part (c), repeat the same steps and mark 115 degrees on the scale, then join the mark to the end point.
Answer: (a) 60 degrees, (b) 30 degrees, (c) 115 degrees, each constructed with a protractor as above.

Worked example: Measure angles and write their names (Exercise 2, Q4)

Step 1: This is a protractor figure activity. Measure each printed angle with a protractor, using the method in Q2.
Step 2: Place the centre point on the vertex and the baseline on the initial ray, then read the measure.
Step 3: Name the angle by its measure: less than 90 degrees is acute.
Step 4: Equal to 90 degrees is right.
Step 5: Greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees is obtuse.
Step 6: Honest note: no text values are printed in the book or in its answer list for this question, so no degree values are given here. Each angle must be measured from its printed figure and then named by the rule in Steps 3 to 5.
Answer: Measure each printed figure with a protractor, then name it acute, right or obtuse by its measure (less than 90 degrees = acute; 90 degrees = right; more than 90 degrees and less than 180 degrees = obtuse).

lessons.title: Exercise 3: Parts of a Circle
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The centre of a circle is the point in the middle of the circle, equally distant from every point on the circle. The radius is a line segment joining the centre to any point on the circle. The diameter is a line segment joining two points on the circle and passing through the centre. Diameter = 2 x radius, so a diameter is made of two radii.

Circle in words: draw a round circle, mark one point in the exact middle and label it Centre; draw a segment from the centre to the edge and label it Radius; draw a segment straight across the circle through the centre, joining two points on the edge, and label it Diameter.

Worked example: Draw the parts of a circle (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: Draw a circle.
Step 2: Mark the centre: the point in the middle of the circle, equally distant from every point on the circle.
Step 3: Draw the radius: a line segment joining the centre to any point on the circle.
Step 4: Draw the diameter: a line segment joining two points on the circle and passing through the centre.
Step 5: Remember that the diameter passes through the centre, and diameter = 2 x radius.
Answer: Centre = the middle point, equally distant from every point on the circle; Radius = segment from the centre to the circle; Diameter = segment joining two points on the circle through the centre.

Step 2: The segments from R to the circle are PR, RQ and RS, so these are the radii.
Step 3: The segment joining two points on the circle through R is PQ, so PQ is the diameter.
Answer: (a) Centre = R, radius = PR, RQ, RS, diameter = PQ.

Worked example: Name the parts of the circles (Exercise 3, Q2b)

Step 1: In figure (b), the middle point is L, so the centre is L.
Step 2: The segments from L to the circle are LJ and LK, so these are the radii.
Step 3: The segment joining two points on the circle through L is JK, so JK is the diameter.
Answer: (b) Centre = L, radius = LJ, LK, diameter = JK.

Worked example: Name the parts of the circles (Exercise 3, Q2c)

Step 1: In figure (c), the middle point is C, so the centre is C.
Step 2: The segments from C to the circle are CD, AC and CB, so these are the radii.
Step 3: The segment joining two points on the circle through C is AB, so AB is the diameter.
Answer: (c) Centre = C, radius = CD, AC, CB, diameter = AB.

lessons.title: Exercise 4: Perimeter and Area on a Square Grid
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a figure. For a figure on a square grid, count or add the lengths of all the sides around the boundary. Area is the space covered by a figure. For a figure on a square grid, area = number of squares covered. For a rectangle or square counted in rows, area = number in one row x number of rows. Perimeter is measured in m or cm; area is measured in square units, written m^2 or cm^2.

Worked example: Perimeter of a 5 m x 5 m square (Exercise 4, Q1a)

Step 1: The figure is a square with each side 5 m.
Step 2: Add all four sides of the boundary: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5.
Step 3: 5 + 5 = 10, 10 + 5 = 15, 15 + 5 = 20.
Answer: Perimeter = 20 m.

Worked example: Perimeter of a 7 cm x 4 cm rectangle (Exercise 4, Q1b)

Step 1: The rectangle has two sides of 7 cm and two sides of 4 cm.
Step 2: Add all four sides: 7 + 4 + 7 + 4.
Step 3: 7 + 4 = 11, 11 + 7 = 18, 18 + 4 = 22.
Answer: Perimeter = 22 cm.

Worked example: Perimeter of a 6 m x 4 m rectangle (Exercise 4, Q1c)

Step 1: The rectangle has two sides of 6 m and two sides of 4 m.
Step 2: Add all four sides: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4.
Step 3: 6 + 4 = 10, 10 + 6 = 16, 16 + 4 = 20.
Answer: Perimeter = 20 m.

Worked example: Area of a 2 x 2 figure (Exercise 4, Q2a)

Step 1: Count the squares: 2 squares in a row and 2 rows.
Step 2: Multiply: 2 x 2 = 4.
Step 3: The unit is cm, so the area is in cm^2.
Answer: Area = 4 cm^2.

Worked example: Area of a 12 x 7 figure (Exercise 4, Q2b)

Step 1: Count the squares: 12 squares in a row and 7 rows.
Step 2: Multiply: 12 x 7 = 84.
Step 3: The unit is m, so the area is in m^2.
Answer: Area = 84 m^2.

Worked example: Area of a 4 x 2 figure (Exercise 4, Q2c)

Step 1: Count the squares: 4 squares in a row and 2 rows.
Step 2: Multiply: 4 x 2 = 8.
Step 3: The unit is cm, so the area is in cm^2.
Answer: Area = 8 cm^2.

Worked example: Area of 1 square (Exercise 4, Q2d)

Step 1: The figure covers only 1 square.
Step 2: So the number of squares covered is 1.
Step 3: The unit is m, so the area is in m^2.
Answer: Area = 1 m^2.

lessons.title: Exercise 5: Line of Symmetry
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A line of symmetry divides a figure into two equal mirror halves. If the figure is folded on the line of symmetry, the two halves match exactly: same shape, same size, but reversed, like a mirror image. A figure may have a line of symmetry or may have none. To complete a figure with respect to its line of symmetry, draw the mirror half on the other side of the line so that both halves match exactly.

Symmetry in words: imagine a figure cut by a dashed line down its middle; the left half and the right half are mirror images of each other across that dashed line.

Worked example: Figures with a line of symmetry (Exercise 5, Q1)

Step 1: Check figure (a): it can be divided by a line into two equal mirror halves.
Step 2: So figure (a) has a line of symmetry.
Step 3: Check figure (b): it can be divided by a line into two equal mirror halves.
Step 4: So figure (b) has a line of symmetry.
Step 5: Check figure (c): no line divides it into two equal mirror halves.
Step 6: So figure (c) has no line of symmetry to mark.
Step 7: Check figure (d): no line divides it into two equal mirror halves.
Step 8: So figure (d) has no line of symmetry to mark.
Answer: The figures with a line of symmetry are (a) and (b).

Worked example: Complete a figure using its line of symmetry (Exercise 5, Q2)

Step 1: Look at the half that is already drawn on one side of the line of symmetry.
Step 2: For each point of the drawn half, mark the mirror point at the same distance on the other side of the line.
Step 3: Join the mirror points in the same order to draw the mirror half.
Step 4: Check that both halves match exactly: same shape, same size, reversed.
Answer: Draw the mirror half on the other side of the line of symmetry so that both halves match exactly (same shape, same size, reversed).

mcqs.why: A line of symmetry divides a figure into two equal mirror halves, one on each side of the line.

lessons.title: Exercise 6: Solid Figures — Vertices, Edges and Surfaces
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A solid figure has vertices (corner points), edges (lines where two surfaces meet) and surfaces (flat or curved faces). Cube: 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 square surfaces. Cuboid: 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 rectangular surfaces. Sphere: 0 vertices, 0 edges, 1 curved surface. Cylinder: 0 vertices, 2 edges, 3 surfaces (1 curved and 2 plane circular). Cone: 1 vertex, 1 edge, 2 surfaces (1 curved and 1 plane circular). Pyramid with a square base: 5 vertices, 8 edges, 5 surfaces (1 square and 4 triangular). To name a solid, count its vertices, edges and surfaces and match the counts to these properties.

Worked example: Name the figures and label vertices, edges and surfaces (Exercise 6, Q1)

Step 1: This question is figure-based: figures (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) are printed figures in the book, so each letter must be matched to its printed figure in the book.
Step 2: For a cube, label 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 square surfaces.
Step 3: For a cuboid, label 8 vertices, 12 edges and 6 rectangular surfaces.
Step 4: For a sphere, label 0 vertices, 0 edges and 1 curved surface.
Step 5: For a cylinder, label 0 vertices, 2 edges and 3 surfaces: 1 curved and 2 plane circular.
Step 6: For a cone, label 1 vertex, 1 edge and 2 surfaces: 1 curved and 1 plane circular.
Step 7: For a pyramid with a square base, label 5 vertices, 8 edges and 5 surfaces: 1 square and 4 triangular.
Step 8: Name each printed figure (a) to (f) by its shape, then label its vertices, edges and surfaces using the counts above.

lessons.title: Exercise 1: Bar Graphs
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A bar graph shows quantities with bars. Always read the scale first: the scale tells how much one square stands for. Then read the height or length of each bar against the scale to find its value. The longest or tallest bar shows the maximum (greatest) value and the shortest bar shows the minimum (smallest) value. To find a total, add all the bar values. To find how much less or more one value is than another, subtract the smaller value from the larger value. All readings below are read from the graphs in the book.

Worked example: Suggested sleep bar graph (Exercise 1, Q1)

Step 1: Read the scale: one horizontal square = 2 hours, as given in the book.
Step 2: Read the bars from the graph in the book: for children of 6 to 12 years, the suggested sleep is 9 hours. This answers part (a).
Step 3: Compare all the bars: the longest bar is for infants, with 14 hours. This is the maximum, answering part (b).
Step 4: For part (c), read the two bars: children of 3 to 5 years sleep 10 hours and children of 13 to 18 years sleep 7 hours.
Step 5: Subtract: 10 - 7 = 3, so the 13 to 18 years sleep is 3 hours less.
Step 6: For part (d), the shortest bar is for children of 13 to 18 years, with 7 hours. This is the minimum.
Answer: (a) 9 hours for 6 to 12 years. (b) Maximum: infants, 14 hours. (c) 3 hours less (10 - 7 = 3). (d) Minimum: 13 to 18 years, 7 hours. All values read from the graph.

Worked example: People who participated in games, April 2020 (Exercise 1, Q2)

Step 1: Read the scale: one vertical square = 10 people, as given in the book.
Step 2: Read each bar from the graph in the book: AJ&K 5, Balochistan 10, Gilgit Baltistan 15, Islamabad 20, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 10, Punjab 40, Sindh 30.
Step 3: For part (a), the tallest bar is Punjab with 40, so the maximum is Punjab, 40 people.
Step 4: For part (b), the shortest bar is AJ&K with 5, so the minimum is AJ&K, 5 people.
Step 5: For part (c), look for the bar with value 30: that bar is Sindh, so 30 people participated from Sindh.
Step 6: For part (d), look for two equal bars: Balochistan 10 and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 10 are equal.
Step 7: For part (e), add all the values: 5 + 10 + 15 + 20 + 10 + 40 + 30.
Step 8: Add in parts: 5 + 10 = 15, 15 + 15 = 30, 30 + 20 = 50, 50 + 10 = 60, 60 + 40 = 100, 100 + 30 = 130.
Answer: (a) Maximum: Punjab, 40 people. (b) Minimum: AJ&K, 5 people. (c) Sindh (30 people). (d) Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 10 each. (e) Total = 130 people. All values read from the graph.

lessons.title: Exercise 2: Line Graphs
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A line graph shows quantities with points joined by a line. Read each point against the scale to find its value. The highest point shows the maximum value and the lowest point shows the minimum value. Points at the same height have the same value. To compare a total for two days with one day, add the two values first, then compare by subtracting. All readings below are read from the line graphs in the book.

Worked example: Customers in a superstore for a week (Exercise 2, Q1)

Step 1: Read each point from the line graph in the book: Monday 700, Tuesday 300, Wednesday 500, Thursday 400, Friday 600, Saturday 900, Sunday 1000.
Step 2: For part (a), the highest point is Sunday with 1000, so the maximum was on Sunday: 1000 customers.
Step 3: For part (b), add Monday and Thursday: 700 + 400 = 1100.
Step 4: Compare with Sunday: 1100 - 1000 = 100, so Monday and Thursday together are more than Sunday by 100.
Step 5: For part (c), the lowest point is Tuesday with 300, so the minimum was on Tuesday: 300 customers.
Step 6: For part (d), read the Friday point: 600 customers came on Friday.
Answer: (a) Maximum: Sunday, 1000 customers. (b) Monday + Thursday = 1100, which is more than Sunday (1000) by 100. (c) Minimum: Tuesday, 300 customers. (d) Friday: 600 customers. All values read from the graph.

Worked example: Maximum temperature in Peshawar for a week of August (Exercise 2, Q2)

Step 1: Read each point from the line graph in the book, in degrees centigrade: Monday 38, Tuesday 36, Wednesday 30, Thursday 35, Friday 35, Saturday 34, Sunday 32.
Step 2: For part (a), the highest point is Monday with 38, so the highest temperature was on Monday: 38 degrees C.
Step 3: For part (b), look for two points at the same height: Thursday 35 and Friday 35 are the same, so Thursday and Friday had the same temperature: 35 degrees C.
Step 4: For part (c), the lowest point is Wednesday with 30, so the lowest temperature was 30 degrees C on Wednesday.
Step 5: For part (d), read the Friday point: the temperature on Friday was 35 degrees C.
Answer: (a) Highest: Monday, 38 degrees C. (b) Thursday and Friday, 35 degrees C each. (c) Lowest: 30 degrees C on Wednesday. (d) Friday: 35 degrees C. All values read from the graph.

lessons.title: Exercise 3: Pie Charts
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A pie chart, also called a circle graph, shows quantities as parts of a circle, with each part labelled with its quantity. Read the label of each part to find its value. The part with the largest label is present in the most amount and the part with the smallest label is present in the least amount. To find a total of two parts, add their labels. To find how much less one part is than another, subtract. To write one part as a fraction of the whole, write: part / total. All readings below are read from the pie charts in the book.

Worked example: Food components in a boiled egg (Exercise 3, Q1)

Step 1: Read each part from the pie chart in the book: Fat 5, Proteins 6, Starch 0.6, Potassium 63, Sodium 62, Cholestrol 187.
Step 2: For part (a), the Fat label is 5, so the quantity of fat is 5.
Step 3: For part (b), the largest label is Cholestrol 187, so Cholestrol is present in the most amount: 187.
Step 4: For part (c), add fat and proteins: 5 + 6 = 11.
Step 5: For part (d), subtract proteins from sodium: 62 - 6 = 56, so proteins are 56 less than sodium.
Step 6: For part (e), the smallest label is Starch 0.6, so Starch is present in the least amount: 0.6.
Answer: (a) Fat = 5. (b) Most: Cholestrol, 187. (c) Fat + proteins = 11. (d) Proteins are 56 less than sodium (62 - 6 = 56). (e) Least: Starch, 0.6. All values read from the pie chart.

Worked example: Cattle bred in a village (Exercise 3, Q2)

Step 1: Read each part from the pie chart in the book: sheep 58, buffaloes 98, goats 100, donkeys 35, bulls 74.
Step 2: Find the total number of cattle: 58 + 98 + 100 + 35 + 74.
Step 3: Add in parts: 58 + 98 = 156, 156 + 100 = 256, 256 + 35 = 291, 291 + 74 = 365. Total = 365.
Step 4: For part (a), the largest value is goats 100, so goats are bred the most: 100.
Step 5: For part (b), the smallest value is donkeys 35, so donkeys are bred the least: 35.
Step 6: For part (c), add sheep and goats: 58 + 100 = 158.
Step 7: Add donkeys and buffaloes: 35 + 98 = 133.
Step 8: Compare: 158 - 133 = 25, so sheep and goats are more by 25.
Step 9: For part (d), write bulls as a fraction of the total: bulls / total = 74/365.
Answer: (a) Most: goats, 100. (b) Least: donkeys, 35. (c) Sheep + goats = 158, donkeys + buffaloes = 133, so sheep and goats are more by 25. (d) Bulls = 74/365 of the total (total = 365). All values read from the pie chart.
